doc:
Package sdb is the API surface handed to Go scripts. A script is a plain
Go file (package main) defining:

	func Run(s *sdb.S) error

It can query any configured connection, loop with parameters, push results
into the results view, and export in any supported format.

funcs.name: IsCanceled

types.name: CopyOpts
types.doc:
CopyOpts shapes s.Copy: destination name, a Where or a whole Query as the
source, a column subset, Create/Truncate of the destination, a per-row
Transform. The zero value copies the whole table into an existing table
of the same name. Set ProgressEvery to have the script output report the
running row count.

fields.name: To
fields.doc: To names the destination table; empty means the source table's name.

fields.name: Query
fields.doc:
Query, when set, is the source instead of a table: any SELECT, with
Args as its parameters. To is then required.

fields.name: Args
fields.doc:
Args are bind parameters for Query or Where, in the source's
placeholder style ($1 Postgres/bytdb, ? MySQL/SQLite).

fields.name: Columns
fields.doc:
Columns limits the copy to these source columns, in this order. The
destination columns have the same names.

fields.name: Where
fields.doc: Where filters the source table's rows: "created_at >= $1".

fields.name: Create
fields.doc:
Create makes the destination table when it does not exist yet. A
Postgres-to-Postgres copy of a table reproduces the source's column
types, NOT NULLs and primary key from the catalog; any other pairing
maps each column to a broad type on the destination (integer, float,
numeric, boolean, date, timestamp, bytes, text). Defaults, indexes
other than the key, and constraints are not copied.

fields.name: Truncate
fields.doc:
Truncate empties the destination first, in the load's transaction:
if the copy fails, the old rows are still there.

fields.name: BatchSize
fields.doc:
BatchSize is rows per INSERT on non-Postgres destinations (see
WriteOptions.BatchSize).

fields.name: Transform
fields.doc:
Transform is called on every row before it is written, and may
change values in place or return a new row of the same length.
Returning a nil row skips it; returning an error stops the copy and
rolls the destination back.

fields.name: Progress
fields.doc:
Progress, when set, is called every ProgressEvery rows (default
100000) with the running total.

types.name: CopyStats
types.doc: CopyStats reports a finished copy; its String() is a one-line summary.

fields.name: From
fields.doc: "conn:table" (or "conn:query")

fields.name: To
fields.doc: "conn:table"

fields.name: Rows
fields.doc: rows loaded

fields.name: Skipped
fields.doc: rows a Transform dropped

fields.name: Direct
fields.doc:
Direct is true when the rows streamed Postgres to Postgres as COPY
text, never decoded into Go values.

types.name: Plan
types.doc:
Plan is an explained statement: its steps (Root, Nodes), what it cost or
took, and dbc's findings about it (Insights). See package explain.

fields.name: Conn
fields.doc: connection name it ran on

fields.name: Statement
fields.doc: the statement explained

fields.name: Command
fields.doc: the EXPLAIN actually sent, for the record

fields.name: Analyzed
fields.doc:
Analyzed: the statement was executed and every step carries measured
rows, loops and time. Measured: the statement was executed and timed
as a whole, on an engine that cannot time its steps (SQLite, bytdb) —
the root carries the total, the steps carry nothing.

fields.name: ResultRows
fields.doc: Measured: the rows the statement returned

fields.name: Notes
fields.doc:
Notes are facts about how the plan was obtained that a reader must
know to read it right ("ran inside a transaction that was rolled
back"). They are not findings about the plan; Insights are.

fields.name: Metric
fields.doc:
Metric is the best measure this plan has, which the views size bars
and flame blocks by unless the user picks another (see Metrics).

fields.name: Raw
fields.doc:
Raw is the engine's own output, verbatim — what "copy the plan"
copies, since that is what a DBA or a search engine recognizes.

methods.name: FileName
methods.doc:
FileName is the name a saved or downloaded rendering of the plan takes:
plan-<conn>-<yyyymmdd-hhmmss>.<ext>, or plan-<stamp>.<ext> with no
connection.

methods.name: Finalize
methods.doc:
Finalize numbers the steps, links parents, derives every computed field
and runs the insight rules. Parsers call it last; it is idempotent, so a
caller that edits a plan (the db layer adding table sizes) calls it again.

Time is the subtle part. Engines report a step's time as an average per
loop, INCLUSIVE of its children, so:

	TotalMs(n) = ActualMs(n) × Loops(n)        (÷ workers inside a Gather)
	SelfMs(n)  = TotalMs(n) − Σ TotalMs(child)  clamped at 0

The clamp matters: a Postgres InitPlan, a CTE referenced twice, or a
parallel child whose per-worker average does not add up can make the naive
difference negative, and a negative bar is worse than a slightly
generous one.

methods.name: Findings
methods.doc:
Findings counts the plan's critical and warning insights — the ones
worth acting on; info-level notes are not counted.

methods.name: HTML
methods.doc:
HTML renders the plan as a self-contained interactive page: a tidy-tree
graph of the steps with heat-colored cards and data-flow edges, a flame
(icicle) view, the insights with copyable fixes, and a detail panel for
the selected step. It references nothing on the network — no CDN, no web
font — so it opens the same from a temp file, an email attachment, or an
air-gapped machine.

The plan travels as the Document JSON (see JSON) inside a
<script type="application/json"> block, parsed by the page at load. That
keeps one source of truth for what a plan contains: the page reads the
same document `dbc explain -t json` prints, weights included, so its bars
and blocks are sized exactly as the terminal's.

methods.name: Headline
methods.doc:
Headline is the plan's one-line summary: engine, how it was obtained, the
totals, the size.

methods.name: JPEG
methods.doc:
JPEG renders the picture as a JPEG. Quality 90 keeps text edges clean;
the flat fills compress well enough that higher buys nothing visible.

methods.name: JSON
methods.doc: JSON renders the plan as an indented Document.

methods.name: Mermaid
methods.doc:
Mermaid renders the plan as a Mermaid flowchart — the form a plan takes in a GitHub or GitLab comment, a wiki page, or a Notion doc, which draw a ```mermaid block as a diagram without anyone installing anything. flowchart BT ┌───────────────┐ n0["Hash Join
…"] │ n0 Hash Join │ ← the root on top n1["Seq Scan · orders
…"] └───────▲───────┘ n1 -->|"36.7k rows"| n0 │ 36.7k rows ┌───────┴───────┐ │ n1 Seq Scan │ └───────────────┘ WHY BOTTOM-TO-TOP. Every other view draws the root on top and the data flowing up into it. In Mermaid an edge A --> B puts B after A in the flow's direction, so "BT" with child --> parent gives the same picture — root on top, arrows pointing the way the rows go — without the reversed arrowheads a TD chart would need. WHAT A NODE SAYS. The same lines the graph's cards carry: the operation and what it works on, the step's most telling detail, rows, and its share of the metric the plan is best measured by. Heat and findings become classDefs (see mermaidClass) so a renderer that draws colors shows where the time goes, and one that does not still has the words. ESCAPING. Labels are double-quoted, and inside one Mermaid reads its own entity codes: #quot; for a quote, and #; for anything else. A plan's text is the user's SQL — full of quotes, <, >, # and | — so every character Mermaid or its HTML labels could read as syntax is written as a code (see mermaidText). The result never breaks the chart, whatever the statement holds.

methods.name: Metrics
methods.doc: Metrics lists the measures this plan can be viewed by, best first.

methods.name: Node
methods.doc: Node returns the step with the given ID, or nil.

methods.name: Nodes
methods.doc:
Nodes returns every step in preorder — a parent before its children,
children in the order the engine listed them — so Nodes()[i].ID == i.

methods.name: PDF
methods.doc:
PDF renders the picture (see picture.go) as a one-page PDF, the page
sized to the picture so nothing is scaled or split: a wide plan makes a
wide page, which a viewer fits to its window and a printer to its paper.

WHY A RASTER INSIDE A PDF, NOT VECTOR PDF. A vector page would need the
text laid out a second time with PDF's own font machinery — embedding
and subsetting the Go fonts as CID fonts to reach beyond Latin-1 — to
draw the same picture the raster already is. At the 2× scale the picture
is drawn at, the page is sharp on screen and on paper; what it gives up
is selecting the text, and the statement and findings are one "copy as
text" away in every dbc view. So the PDF is a thin, dependency-free
wrapper, written by hand below, around the tested renderer.

The file, object by object:

	1 Catalog ─► 2 Pages ─► 3 Page ─┬─► 4 content stream: "q W 0 0 H 0 0 cm /Im0 Do Q"
	                                └─► 5 Image XObject (RGB, Flate + PNG "Up" predictor)
	6 Info (Title, Creator, CreationDate)
	xref table, trailer

The image is Flate-compressed after the PNG "Up" filter (each row stored
as its difference from the row above). The picture is mostly flat fills,
so most rows are all zeros after the filter and compress to almost
nothing; plain Flate on raw pixels is several times larger.

methods.name: PNG
methods.doc:
PNG renders the picture as a PNG: lossless, and for a picture of flat
fills and text usually smaller than the JPEG too.

methods.name: Picture
methods.doc: Picture draws the plan. See the top of this file for what is on it.

methods.name: ResolveAliases
methods.doc:
ResolveAliases fills in the table behind each step that names only an
alias, from the statement's FROM and JOIN clauses, then re-runs the rules
so their suggestions can name real tables.

methods.name: Share
methods.doc: Share is the step's Self as a fraction (0–1) of the whole plan's.

methods.name: Text
methods.doc:
Text renders the plan as an indented tree with a column of numbers and a
bar per step — the headless `dbc explain` output, the "copy plan as text"
clipboard payload, and what the assistant is shown.

	Hash Join · (o.user_id = u.id)             36,650 rows          8.4 ms  31% ███▏
	├─ Bitmap Heap Scan · orders o             50,000 rows          6.2 ms  23% ██▎
	│  └─ Bitmap Index Scan · orders_status    50,000 rows          0.9 ms   3% ▎
	└─ Hash                                    15,659 rows          2.3 ms   9% ▉

The bar and percentage are each step's OWN share (self time, self cost),
so they add up to 100% down the column and point straight at the step
that matters; the tree lines carry the nesting.

methods.name: WriteFile
methods.sig: func (p *Plan) WriteFile(dir, ext string, data []byte) (string, error)
methods.doc:
WriteFile saves one rendering of the plan (the page, a PDF, a JPEG, the
Mermaid source) into dir under the same what-and-when name WriteHTML
uses, with ext as its extension, and returns its path. 0600 for the
reason WriteHTML gives: every rendering quotes the statement.

methods.name: WriteHTML
methods.doc:
WriteHTML saves the interactive page into dir (created if need be) under a
name that says what and when — plan-<conn>-<yyyymmdd-hhmmss>.html — and
returns its path. The file is 0600: a plan quotes the statement and its
literals, which are the user's business, and dir is usually the shared
temp directory.

types.name: PlanText
types.doc:
PlanText shapes Plan.Text: width, the metric bars are sized by, color,
and whether the findings are appended.

fields.name: Width
fields.doc: total line width; 0 = 100

fields.name: Metric
fields.doc: "" = the plan's best

fields.name: Color
fields.doc: ANSI colors, for a terminal

fields.name: Insights
fields.doc: append the findings

types.name: Reader
types.doc:
Reader streams a query's rows: for rd.Next() { row := rd.Row() }, then
rd.Err(). Close it (defer rd.Close()) if you stop before the end.

methods.name: Close
methods.doc:
Close releases the query's connection. It is safe to call more than once,
and a deferred Close after reading to the end costs nothing.

methods.name: Columns
methods.doc: Columns returns the result's column names.

methods.name: Count
methods.doc: Count is the number of rows read so far.

methods.name: DBTypes
methods.doc:
DBTypes returns the driver's type name for each column, upper case
("INT4", "TEXT", "DATETIME"); empty where the driver does not say.

methods.name: Err
methods.doc: Err returns the error that stopped Next early, if any.

methods.name: Next
methods.doc:
Next advances to the next row, reporting false at the end or on an error
(see Err). The Reader closes itself when it runs out.

methods.name: Row
methods.doc: Row returns the current row. Each call to Next makes a new slice.

types.name: Result
types.doc: Result is the tabular result type scripts receive from Query.

fields.name: Conn
fields.doc: connection name the statement ran on

fields.name: Query
fields.doc: the statement text

fields.name: Columns
fields.doc: column names

fields.name: Rows
fields.doc: display-ready values (NULL rendered as "NULL")

fields.name: Raw
fields.doc: typed values, used for JSON export

fields.name: Duration
fields.doc: wall time for the statement

fields.name: Truncated
fields.doc: true when the row limit was hit

fields.name: IsExec
fields.doc: true for non-query statements (INSERT/UPDATE/...)

fields.name: Affected
fields.doc: rows affected, when IsExec

fields.name: Transposed
fields.doc:
Transposed marks a result turned on its side (export.Transpose): each
row is one of the source's columns, its name in column 0, so the HTML
renderings draw that column as row headers rather than as data.

methods.name: RowCount
methods.doc: RowCount returns the number of data rows.

types.name: S
types.doc: S is the session handle passed to a script's Run function.

methods.name: Canceled
methods.doc: Canceled reports whether the user has stopped this run.

methods.name: Conns
methods.doc: Conns returns the configured connection names.

methods.name: Copy
methods.sig: func (s *S) Copy(src, dst, table string, opt CopyOpts) (CopyStats, error)
methods.doc:
Copy copies table from connection src into connection dst:

	st, err := s.Copy("prod", "local", "public.orders", sdb.CopyOpts{
		Create: true, Truncate: true, Where: "created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'",
	})
	s.Print("%s", st) // copied 48213 rows prod:public.orders → local:public.orders in 1.4s (direct COPY)

Postgres to Postgres without a Transform or Args streams COPY to COPY and
never decodes a row; every other pairing goes row by row. Either way the
destination is loaded in one transaction (with its Create and Truncate),
so a failed or stopped copy leaves it as it was.

methods.name: Ctx
methods.doc:
Ctx returns the session's context. Long-running scripts can select on
s.Ctx().Done() (or check s.Canceled()) to bail out early.

methods.name: DB
methods.doc:
DB exposes the raw *database/sql.DB for a connection — the escape hatch
for transactions, prepared statements, or anything else database/sql can do.

methods.name: Exec
methods.sig: func (s *S) Exec(conn, stmt string, args ...any) (int64, error)
methods.doc:
Exec runs a non-query statement and returns the rows affected. Its server
notices are printed as Query's are.

methods.name: Explain
methods.sig: func (s *S) Explain(conn, stmt string, analyze bool) (*Plan, error)
methods.doc:
Explain describes how conn's database runs stmt, as the TUI's Ctrl+X and
`dbc explain` do. analyze runs the statement to measure it: on Postgres a
write is analyzed inside a transaction that is rolled back; on the other
engines a write is explained but not run. It runs on its own session, not
one the script shares with Query.

	p, err := s.Explain("pg", "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42", true)
	s.Print("%s", p.Text(sdb.PlanText{Insights: true}))
	for _, in := range p.Insights { if in.Severity != "info" { … } }

methods.name: Export
methods.sig: func (s *S) Export(r *Result, format, path string) error
methods.doc:
Export renders a result in the named format (csv|tsv|markdown|html|json|text)
and writes it to path — or to the system clipboard when path is empty.

methods.name: Print
methods.doc: Print writes a Printf-style message to the script output.

methods.name: Query
methods.sig: func (s *S) Query(conn, query string, args ...any) (*Result, error)
methods.doc:
Query runs a statement with parameters on the named connection and
returns the result set. Use the placeholder style of the target driver
($1 for postgres/bytdb, ? for mysql/sqlite).

Server notices the statement raises (Postgres RAISE NOTICE and its kin)
are written to the script output, as Print does, before Query returns —
whether or not the statement failed.

methods.name: Reader
methods.sig: func (s *S) Reader(conn, query string, args ...any) (*Reader, error)
methods.doc:
Reader runs query on conn and streams its rows. Use the placeholder style
of the connection's driver ($1 postgres/bytdb, ? mysql/sqlite).

methods.name: Show
methods.doc: Show pushes a result to the results view (TUI) or prints it (headless).

methods.name: Writer
methods.sig: func (s *S) Writer(conn, table string, cols []string, opt WriteOpts) (*Writer, error)
methods.doc:
Writer starts a load into table on conn; rows passed to Write line up
with cols. Nothing is visible to other sessions until Close commits.

types.name: WriteOpts
types.doc:
WriteOpts shapes s.Writer: Setup statements and Truncate run first, in
the load's transaction; BatchSize tunes INSERT batching off Postgres.

fields.name: Setup
fields.doc:
Setup statements run first, inside the load's transaction — a CREATE
TABLE, an ALTER, a DELETE of the slice being reloaded. If the load
fails they are rolled back with it (except where the engine commits
DDL on its own: MySQL).

fields.name: Truncate
fields.doc:
Truncate empties the table after Setup and before the first row, in
the same transaction: a reload either replaces the old rows or leaves
them alone, never a half-empty table.

fields.name: BatchSize
fields.doc:
BatchSize is rows per INSERT statement on engines loaded by INSERT
(everything but Postgres). 0 means 500. It is lowered automatically so
one statement stays under the engines' bind-parameter limits.

types.name: Writer
types.doc:
Writer loads rows into one table in one transaction: w.Write(row) per
row, then w.Close() to commit. defer w.Abort() rolls back on any early
return; it is a no-op after Close.

methods.name: Abort
methods.doc:
Abort rolls the load back. It is a no-op after Close or a previous Abort,
so `defer w.Abort()` is the idiom that guarantees an early return or a
panic never leaves a transaction open.

methods.name: Close
methods.doc:
Close sends any buffered rows and commits, returning the rows loaded.
After a failed Write it rolls back instead and returns that failure.

methods.name: Columns
methods.doc: Columns returns the column list rows are written in.

methods.name: Count
methods.doc: Count is the number of rows accepted by Write so far.

methods.name: Write
methods.doc:
Write queues one row; its values line up with Columns. A failure aborts
the whole load, and every later Write or Close returns the same error.
